title: The origins of cinema

paragraphs.text: Many consider that the history of motion pictures began in 1824, when the British doctor Peter Mark Roget described an optical effect he called persistence of vision – the illusion of movement created when a series of still pictures are set into motion. Over the next decades, this idea inspired a number of simple optical toys and mechanical inventions related to motion and vision. One of the most significant was created in 1834 by the British inventor William George Horner. Originally called a Daedalum, but better known by its later name of Zoetrope, Horner's device consisted of a hollow drum, rotated by means of a crank. Around the drum's inner surface was a strip of paper with a sequence of paintings, drawings or illustrations on it. As the device turned, the viewer could observe the illusion of moving images through regularly spaced narrow slits.

The development of still photography in the mid-19th century led to the creation of a number of variations on the Zoetrope. In 1861, the US inventor Coleman Sellers patented the Kinematoscope, a device containing a sequence of stereoscopic (3D) photos on glass plates, in a rotating box. 1870 saw the first public demonstrations of US inventor Henry Renno Heyl's Phasmatrope, one of the earliest devices to show apparently 'moving' photographs. On February 5th of that year, Heyl delighted audiences at the Academy of Music in Philadelphia with his photographs of dancers, shown in rapid succession so as to create the impression of motion.

The next step in the history of motion pictures was the invention of the Praxinoscope. Devised in 1877 by Frenchman Charles Emile Reynaud, this refined version of the Zoetrope had mirrors at the centre of the drum. This was followed in 1879 by the British photographer Eadweard Muybridge's invention of the Zoopraxiscope. Also known as 'the wheel of life', this machine recreated the illusion of movement. Images appeared on a screen, having been projected from a series of photos printed on a disc that turned when the machine was operating.

However, true motion pictures, rather than eye-fooling 'animations', could only occur after the development of a flexible film capable of recording split-second pictures. In 1882, French innovator and physiologist Etienne-Jules Marey, often regarded as the ‘inventor of cinema’, constructed a camera (or 'photographic gun') that could take 12 photographs per second. Marey's 'chronophotographs', as he called them, were revolutionary, and he was soon able to achieve a rate of 30 images per second. Further experimentation was conducted by French-born Louis Aimé Augustin Le Prince, who used long rolls of paper covered with photographic emulsion for a camera that he devised and patented. A few seconds of his 1888 motion picture film entitled 'Traffic Crossing Leeds Bridge' still survive.

In November 1890, William Dickson, the young British assistant of the famed US inventor Thomas Edison, devised a simple but ingenious motor-powered motion-picture camera known as the Kinetograph. This used 35mm-wide film made out of celluloid, a newly developed synthetic gelatin-coated material which was transparent, strong, and flexible. Officially launched in 1892, Dickson's camera featured an innovative system of sprockets (teeth on a moving wheel) that connected with sprocket holes in the celluloid, and advanced the film. The sprocket system would momentarily pause the film before the camera's shutter to create a photographic frame (a still or photographic image). Although its bulky motor was soon to be replaced with a lightweight hand-crank mechanism, the Kinetograph set the standard for the motion picture cameras that would be used for the next century.

Dickson also designed an early version of a movie-picture projector called the Kinetoscope. Around that same time, he filmed his first experimental Kinetoscope trial film, 'Monkeyshines No 1'; the only surviving film from the cylinder Kinetoscope, and apparently the first motion picture ever produced on photographic film in the United States. It features the movement of laboratory assistant Sacco Albanese, filmed with a system using tiny images that rotate around the cylinder.

Meanwhile in Lyons, France, brothers Louis and Auguste Lumière, often called the founding fathers of modern film, were inspired by Edison and Dickson's work. They created their own portable, hand-held device, known as the Cinematographe, patented in February 1895. This multi-purpose device, which combined camera, printer and projecting capabilities, was more profitable than Edison and Dickson's model, because a number of spectators could watch the film on a large screen at the same time. On December 28, 1895, the Lumières presented the first commercial exhibition of a projected motion picture to a paying public in the world's first movie theatre – in the Salon Indien, at the Grand Café on the Boulevard des Capucines in Paris. Cinema – a word derived from Cinematographe – had finally arrived.
